Chapter 12: The Lantern Keeper

Updated 3 days ago · 1,204 words

The lantern keeper lived at the end of the harbour wall, in a hut built from the timbers of a boat that had not come home. Every evening he walked the length of the wall with a long pole and a box of matches, and every morning he walked it again to put the lanterns out, and in between he sat at his window and watched the water as if it owed him money.

12

“You're late,” he said when Mei came in without knocking.

3

“The tide was early.”

1

“The tide is never early. People are late and blame the sea for it.”

She put the basket on his table and began to unpack it, the bread first and then the fish wrapped in newspaper, and he watched her do it without offering to help, the way he had watched her mother do it for twenty years before her. When the basket was empty she folded the cloth and sat down across from him, and for a while neither of them said anything at all.

Chapter 13: Low Water

Updated 2 days ago · 987 words

At low water the harbour showed its bones. The keeper said the old town was down there under the mud, the whole of it, streets and chapel and all, and that on the lowest tide of the year you could walk out to the chapel door if you knew where to put your feet and did not mind the cold. Mei had heard the story since she was small and had never once believed it.

“Tonight,” he said. “The lowest one.”

She laughed, and then she saw that he was already putting on his boots.
